notice: Browser simulator with recorded outputs. No cluster is contacted. Commands are validated locally so you can practise the exact workflow safely.

labs.title: First contact with a cluster
labs.brief: Learn the three commands every Kubernetes session starts with: version, nodes, and pods.
labs.objective: Read cluster state without changing anything.

steps.task: Print the client and server Kubernetes version.
steps.explain: kubectl version reports the client build and, when a cluster is reachable, the API server build. Version skew matters during upgrades.
steps.output:
Client Version: v1.32.2
Kustomize Version: v5.6.0
Server Version: v1.32.2

steps.task: List the cluster nodes.
steps.explain: Nodes are the machines that run pods. The control plane schedules work onto them and reports their readiness.
steps.output:
NAME           STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
controlplane   Ready    control-plane   19d   v1.32.2
node01         Ready    <none>          19d   v1.32.2

steps.task: List pods in all namespaces.
steps.explain: Without -A you only see the current namespace. Cluster-wide inventory is the first step in almost every troubleshooting flow.
steps.output:
NAMESPACE     NAME                                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
kube-system   coredns-7db6d8ff4d-2xk9p              1/1     Running   0          19d
kube-system   etcd-controlplane                     1/1     Running   2          19d
kube-system   kube-apiserver-controlplane           1/1     Running   2          19d
kube-system   kube-proxy-node01                     1/1     Running   0          19d
default       web-6f7c9b8d4f-9q2mv                  1/1     Running   0          4d

labs.title: Create a namespace and a pod
labs.brief: Scope your work in a namespace, then run a single NGINX pod imperatively.
labs.objective: Create a namespace, launch a pod, and confirm it is running.

steps.task: Create a namespace named devops-lab.
steps.explain: Namespaces group objects and provide a scope for names, quotas, and RBAC. Creating one first keeps experiments isolated.
steps.output: namespace/devops-lab created

steps.task: Run a pod named web using nginx:1.27 in the devops-lab namespace.
steps.explain: kubectl run creates a single pod. In real work a Deployment is preferred because it adds self-healing and rollout control.
steps.output: pod/web created

steps.task: Confirm the pod is Running in devops-lab.
steps.explain: READY 1/1 and STATUS Running mean the container started and passed its readiness gate. It does not prove the app works.
steps.output:
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web    1/1     Running   0          12s

labs.title: Expose a pod with a Service
labs.brief: Give a pod a stable network identity and inspect the resulting service.
labs.objective: Create a NodePort service and read its allocated port.

steps.task: Expose the web pod on port 80 as a NodePort service in devops-lab.
steps.explain: A Service selects pods by label and forwards traffic to them. NodePort additionally opens a port on every node.
steps.output: service/web-svc exposed

steps.task: Show the service and its NodePort.
steps.explain: The PORT(S) column shows clusterIP:port and the node port after the colon. Clients outside the cluster use nodeIP:nodePort.
steps.output:
NAME      TYPE       CLUSTER-IP      EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)        AGE
web-svc   NodePort   10.96.184.201   <none>        80:31284/TCP   9s

steps.task: Print the endpoints selected by the service.
steps.explain: Endpoints are the pod IPs behind a service. If the list is empty, the selector does not match any ready pod.
steps.output:
NAME      ENDPOINTS        AGE
web-svc   10.244.1.17:80   42s

labs.title: Troubleshoot with logs and describe
labs.brief: Follow the evidence trail: events first, logs second.
labs.objective: Read pod events and filter logs for errors.

steps.task: Describe the web pod in devops-lab.
steps.explain: The Events section at the bottom explains scheduling, image pulls, and probe failures. Read it before guessing.
steps.output:
Name:             web
Namespace:        devops-lab
Node:             node01/172.30.2.2
Status:           Running
Events:
  Type    Reason     Age   From               Message
  ----    ------     ----  ----               -------
  Normal  Scheduled  92s   default-scheduler  Successfully assigned devops-lab/web to node01
  Normal  Pulled     91s   kubelet            Container image "nginx:1.27" already present on machine
  Normal  Started    90s   kubelet            Started container web

steps.task: Show the last 50 log lines from the web container.
steps.explain: --tail limits output so a noisy container does not flood your terminal. Combine with grep when you know the signal.

labs.title: Ship a change, then roll it back
labs.brief: Change an image, watch the rollout, and undo it without drama.
labs.objective: Use rollout status and rollout undo with confidence.

steps.task: Update the web Deployment image to nginx:1.27-alpine.
steps.hint: kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27-alpine -n devops-lab
steps.explain: Changing the pod template creates a new ReplicaSet. The Deployment gradually shifts traffic as new pods become ready.
steps.output: deployment.apps/web image updated

steps.task: Watch the rollout finish.
steps.explain: rollout status blocks until the update completes or fails, which makes it safe to use in scripts and CI.
steps.output:
Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 1 out of 2 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 2 out of 2 new replicas have been updated...
deployment "web" successfully rolled out

steps.task: Roll the Deployment back to the previous revision.
steps.explain: rollout undo restores the previous ReplicaSet. The Deployment keeps history, so recovery is one command, not a rebuild.
steps.output: deployment.apps/web rolled back

steps.task: Show the rollout history for the Deployment.
steps.explain: History lists revisions. Add --revision=N to inspect the pod template behind a specific revision.
steps.output:
deployment.apps/web
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
2         <none>
3         <none>

labs.title: Find the resource hog
labs.brief: Use metrics to find which pod and node are under pressure.
labs.objective: Read top output and sort by memory.

steps.task: Show memory usage for pods across all namespaces, highest first.
steps.explain: kubectl top requires the metrics-server. Sorting by memory turns a wall of numbers into a ranked list.
steps.output:
NAMESPACE     NAME                          CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
default       analytics-7c9f8d6b5-4nq2p     182m         1.4Gi
kube-system   etcd-controlplane             41m          412Mi
default       web-6f7c9b8d4f-9q2mv          3m           38Mi

steps.task: Show node resource usage.
steps.explain: Node metrics show cluster-wide pressure. A pod can be healthy while the node it sits on is near capacity.
steps.output:
NAME           CPU(cores)   CPU(%)   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY(%)
controlplane   212m         10%      1.2Gi           62%
node01         640m         32%      3.8Gi           78%

labs.title: Ansible: ping, then converge
labs.brief: Verify connectivity, check a playbook, and run it against inventory.
labs.objective: Use ansible and ansible-playbook against a real inventory file.

steps.task: Ping all hosts in the inventory.
steps.explain: The ping module is not ICMP. It opens an SSH session and runs a tiny Python probe, proving authentication and Python are ready.

steps.task: Run a syntax check on basic-playbook.yml with the inventory.
steps.explain: A syntax check parses the playbook without touching hosts. It catches YAML and module-name mistakes before they reach production.
steps.output: playbook: basic-playbook.yml

steps.task: Run basic-playbook.yml against the inventory.
steps.explain: The PLAY RECAP is the source of truth: ok, changed, unreachable, failed. A green recap with changed=1 means the system moved toward the desired state once.

labs.title: Ansible: users, groups, and validation
labs.brief: Run a user-management playbook and verify the result from the control node.
labs.objective: Understand loops, password hashes, and ad-hoc validation.

steps.task: Run create-users-and-groups.yaml with the inventory.
steps.explain: The play loops over users and applies group, home, and password settings. Fixed salts are required for true idempotency.
steps.output:
PLAY [Ansbile Add User & Group] ************************************************

TASK [Creating Admin Groups] ***************************************************
changed: [stapp01]

TASK [Creating Dev Groups] *****************************************************
changed: [stapp01]

TASK [Creating Admins Group Users] *********************************************
changed: [stapp01] => (item=rob)
changed: [stapp01] => (item=joy)
changed: [stapp01] => (item=david)

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
stapp01                    : ok=6    changed=5    unreachable=0    failed=0

steps.task: Validate that user rob exists on stapp01.
steps.explain: Ad-hoc commands are perfect for read-only verification. id rob proves the user and group membership without another playbook.
steps.output:
stapp01 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
uid=1002(rob) gid=1003(admins) groups=1003(admins),10(wheel)

labs.title: Puppet: noop, apply, verify
labs.brief: Preview a catalog change, apply it, then prove NGINX is installed.

steps.task: Preview install-package.pp without changing the system.
steps.explain: --noop compiles and compares the catalog but makes no changes. It is the Puppet equivalent of a dry run.
steps.output:
Notice: Compiled catalog for node01 in environment production in 0.08 seconds
Notice: /Stage[main]/Main/Package[nginx]/ensure: current_value absent, should be installed (noop)
Notice: Class[Main]: Would have triggered 'refresh' from 1 event
Notice: Applied catalog in 0.11 seconds

steps.task: Apply install-package.pp for real.
steps.explain: Apply converges the system. The first run installs NGINX; a second run should report no changes, demonstrating idempotency.
steps.output:
Notice: Compiled catalog for node01 in environment production in 0.07 seconds
Notice: /Stage[main]/Main/Package[nginx]/ensure: created
Notice: Applied catalog in 6.42 seconds

steps.task: Verify the installed NGINX package version.
steps.explain: Verification is separate from configuration. Always check the observed state instead of trusting the tool's success message.

labs.title: Security: scan before you deploy
labs.brief: Scan an image, read the critical count, and inspect what is actually running.
labs.objective: Make image risk visible before it reaches the cluster.

steps.task: Scan nginx:1.27 for vulnerabilities with Trivy.
steps.explain: Trivy reports vulnerabilities by package and severity. The critical count is a fast triage signal, not the whole risk picture.

steps.task: Show the running Deployment image in JSON.
steps.explain: Reading the live object proves which image actually runs. Tags can move; digests do not.

labs.title: CKA: jsonpath and filtered logs
labs.brief: Extract exactly one field, then save only the evidence you need.
labs.objective: Practise the two most common exam output tricks.

steps.task: Print only the first targetPort of service web-svc.
steps.explain: jsonpath avoids parsing human-formatted tables. Quote the expression so the shell does not expand braces.

steps.task: Save only ERROR lines from pod web to errors.log.
steps.hint: kubectl logs web -n devops-lab | grep ERROR > errors.log
steps.explain: The exam asks for a specific artifact. Filtering and redirecting produces exactly that file without noise.
steps.output: errors.log created (3 matching lines)

labs.title: Deploy the Guestbook stack
labs.brief: Apply a multi-tier app and verify every layer comes up.
labs.objective: Read a multi-document manifest and check the rollout.

steps.task: Apply all guestbook manifests in the directory.
steps.explain: kubectl apply -f on a directory reads every YAML file. Ordering is handled by the API server, but dependencies still matter at runtime.
steps.output:
deployment.apps/redis-master created
service/redis-master created
deployment.apps/redis-slave created
service/redis-slave created
deployment.apps/frontend created
service/frontend created

steps.task: Watch the frontend rollout complete.
steps.explain: The frontend depends on Redis. A rollout can succeed while the app still fails, so check logs and endpoints next.
steps.output:
Waiting for deployment "frontend" rollout to finish: 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
deployment "frontend" successfully rolled out

steps.task: List the services to find the frontend NodePort.
steps.explain: The frontend Service exposes the app. NodePort is for labs; production usually uses an Ingress or LoadBalancer.
steps.output:
